common_name: Fishbone Cactus (Ric Rac Cactus, Zig-Zag Cactus)

planting.note: Root stem-segment cuttings in spring or summer after allowing the cut end to callus for a day or two, then set in a fast-draining orchid-bark-based cactus mix in bright indirect light; this epiphyte grows naturally on trees and rocks in Mexican cloud forests and resents both direct sun and soggy roots.

directions: Grow in a well-drained, chunky orchid-bark or cactus potting mix in bright indirect light, never full sun, which quickly scorches the flattened stems. The strongly toothed, zig-zagging stem margins that give this jungle cactus its common name are a striking year-round feature, and in fall mature plants produce large, fragrant, pale pink to white flowers that open at night along the notches of the stems. As an epiphyte from tropical Mexican forest canopies, it prefers higher humidity and more regular moisture than desert cacti, though the top inch of mix should still dry between waterings to prevent stem rot. It is superb in a hanging basket or on a high shelf where its cascading stems can trail freely.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root two- or three-segment stem cuttings after a brief callusing period in a well-drained, humus-rich orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light; like its relatives, this epiphyte needs several weeks of cool nights and uninterrupted darkness in autumn to trigger the following spring's flower buds.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained potting mix amended with orchid bark, and keep evenly moist during active growth while letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. Native to the shaded branches and rock crevices of the Brazilian Atlantic coastal rainforest, this cactus carries flattened, scalloped stem segments that erupt in late winter to spring with vivid star-shaped flowers in red, pink, orange, or white, timed around the Easter holiday in temperate climates. Flower bud formation depends on a cool, dry autumn rest of six to eight weeks with nighttime temperatures near 50-55 degrees F and long uninterrupted nights, much like its Thanksgiving and Christmas cactus relatives. Keep it away from heating vents, cold drafts, and direct sun, all of which cause bud or segment drop.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root a mature, callused stem cutting in a fast-draining, chunky orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light; keep slightly root-bound in a fairly small pot, since these jungle-cactus hybrids often flower more reliably when their roots are somewhat crowded.

directions: Grow in a fast-draining, humus-rich orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light, with only gentle early-morning direct sun tolerated in mild climates. These sprawling, flat- or triangular-stemmed hybrids descend from generations of breeding among wild epiphytic jungle cacti, chiefly Epiphyllum, Disocactus, and Selenicereus species from Central and South American rainforest canopies, and are grown almost entirely for their spectacular flowers, which can reach 6-10 inches across in nearly every color but true blue. Each bloom typically lasts only a day or two in late spring or summer, so many growers track bud development closely to catch the show. Feed lightly with a diluted bloom-boosting fertilizer during the growing season, water thoroughly and then allow the mix to dry somewhat before watering again, and protect from frost, since this tender hybrid is grown outdoors year-round only in zone 10-11 and elsewhere as a container or greenhouse plant.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Break off and callus a rooted offset or stem cutting for a day or two, then set shallowly in a very gritty, fast-draining cactus mix in bright light with some protection from harsh midday sun; established clumps can also be divided at the same time of year.

directions: Plant in a very gritty, fast-draining cactus mix in bright light, with light shade from the most intense midday sun in hot climates. This low, clustering South African succulent forms mats of soft, toothed, four- to five-angled stems and produces unusual star-shaped flowers banded in maroon and cream-yellow, each with a raised, ring-like center that resembles a lifesaver candy, giving the plant both of its common names. The blooms release a faint carrion scent to attract fly pollinators rather than bees. Water sparingly, letting the mix dry completely between waterings, since the shallow root system rots quickly in wet, poorly drained soil; grow as a container or houseplant outside of zone 9b-11, bringing it indoors well before frost.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
University of California Cooperative Extension — Succulents

planting.note: Lay or lightly bury stem cuttings on top of a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in spring or summer in bright indirect light to partial sun; roots form readily along the stem nodes within a few weeks.

directions: Grow in a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, watering only once the soil has dried completely. This South African trailer is a close relative of string of pearls but carries small, curved, banana-shaped succulent leaves along thin, fast-growing stems that can trail 2-3 feet from a hanging basket or shelf edge. In late winter to spring it can produce small, white, cinnamon-scented daisy-like flowers. It grows noticeably faster and is somewhat more forgiving of brighter light than string of pearls, but shares the same intolerance for wet feet, so err on the side of underwatering. All parts are considered toxic if ingested by pets or people.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: String of Raindrops (String of Watermelons, String of Gooseberries)

planting.note: Lay stem cuttings on the surface of a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in spring or summer in bright indirect light to partial sun and mist lightly until roots establish along the buried nodes.

directions: Grow in a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, allowing the mix to dry fully before watering again. Trailing stems carry plump, teardrop-shaped leaves with fine translucent striping reminiscent of tiny watermelons, a South African relative of string of pearls that is somewhat larger-leaved, faster growing, and slightly more tolerant of brighter light. Clusters of small white, faintly fragrant flowers can appear in winter on mature plants. As with its relatives, overwatering and poorly drained soil are the most common causes of failure, so keep it on the dry side, especially in winter when growth slows.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: String of Dolphins (Dolphin Plant, Dolphin Necklace)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring or summer in a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light to partial sun after allowing the cut ends to callus for a day; this hybrid roots slower than string of pearls, so keep the mix barely moist, not wet, until new growth appears.

directions: Grow in a very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light to partial sun, watering only when the mix has dried completely. This whimsical intergeneric hybrid, a cross between string of pearls and the candle plant (Curio articulatus), bears crescent-shaped, faintly ribbed leaves that curve like a pod of leaping dolphins along trailing stems, making it a favorite conversation piece for hanging baskets and shelves. It shares the low-water, fast-draining needs of both parents and rots quickly if left in soggy mix, so let it dry out fully between waterings, especially in winter. As with its string-of-pearls parent, it is considered toxic if ingested by pets.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Thanksgiving Cactus (Crab Cactus, False Christmas Cactus)

planting.note: Root two- or three-segment stem cuttings after callusing for a day or two in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix in bright indirect light; in autumn, give the plant roughly six weeks of long uninterrupted nights and cool temperatures near 50-55 degrees F to initiate flower buds.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in a well-drained, humus-rich potting mix, keeping it evenly moist during active growth and allowing the surface to dry slightly between waterings. This Brazilian rainforest epiphyte carries flattened, jointed stem segments with pointed, claw-like serrated edges, the feature that distinguishes it from the smoother-scalloped true Christmas cactus, Schlumbergera x buckleyi; most cactus plants sold in stores in November and December under the name Christmas cactus are actually this earlier-blooming species. Vivid pink, red, orange, purple, or white flowers dangle from the segment tips once the plant has had a cool, short-day autumn rest. Keep it away from cold drafts, heating vents, and sudden temperature swings, which can cause buds and even whole segments to drop.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Root small clusters of stem segments after a brief callusing period in a loose, well-drained orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light to light shade; this epiphyte grows on trees and rocks in humid South American forests and tolerates lower light better than most cacti.

directions: Grow in a loose, well-drained orchid-bark cactus mix in bright indirect light to light shade, keeping it lightly moist and misting occasionally to mimic its humid native habitat. Native to the rainforest canopies of Brazil and Argentina, this spineless jungle cactus branches profusely into dense, airy clusters of tiny cylindrical, rice-grain-like segments, giving mature plants a soft, coral-like texture that spills attractively over a hanging basket rim. Small cream-white flowers appear along the stems in spring, followed by translucent pinkish-white berries. It is more shade-tolerant and humidity-loving than most cacti and should never be allowed to dry out completely for long periods, though standing water and heavy, poorly drained soil will still cause stem rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
